Expose liveness/readiness endpoints through ASP.NET Core health checks
(`health-check` skill) and prefer native HTTP probes supplied by the
orchestrator. Do not assume the runtime image contains `curl`, `wget`, or shell
utilities; if Compose must run an in-container health command, verify the
executable exists or add an appropriate probe mechanism, weighing the cost of
installing debugging packages into a production image.

## Angular Container

When the Angular frontend is deployed as a static application, build it in a Node
build stage and serve the generated assets with the selected hosting strategy.
Nginx is not mandatory; the platform may provide static hosting directly. Keep
API base URLs and environment configuration compatible with the deployment
strategy.

## `.dockerignore`

Exclude files that do not belong in the build context:

```text
.git
.vs
**/bin
**/obj
**/node_modules
TestResults
coverage
```

Do not exclude tests when the image build intentionally runs them, and never
exclude files required by restore/build.

## Image Optimization

Start with standard supported .NET runtime images. Consider Alpine, chiseled
images, trimming, Native AOT, or other size optimizations only when
compatibility and deployment requirements justify them, and verify
globalization, native dependencies, reflection, diagnostics, and other runtime
behavior when using specialized images.

A lightweight connectivity/availability check — no expensive business queries,
large scans, or data modification. Use provider/framework health-check
integration where suitable.

Check an external dependency only when its availability matters to the meaning
of readiness. Avoid readiness cascades (service A readiness → calls service B
readiness → calls service C …) without understanding the operational
consequences; prefer a lightweight check of the capability actually needed.

## Status Codes

Health endpoints return success when healthy and a non-success status when
unhealthy according to the configured probe policy; `HealthCheckOptions` allows
status-code mapping. Do not reuse business API status semantics mechanically for
orchestrator probes.

## Response Body

Keep probe responses small. When operators need detailed diagnostics, protect
that endpoint with network or authorization controls appropriate to the
environment.

## Exposure

Health endpoints often must be reachable by infrastructure without ordinary user
authentication. Choose exposure from the deployment topology: private/internal
network access, a dedicated management port, host restrictions, or authorization
where the probe infrastructure supports it.

## Startup Readiness

If initialization is asynchronous or slow, keep readiness unhealthy until the
required startup work has completed.

## Performance

Health checks may run frequently. Avoid expensive queries, long external
timeouts, large allocations, full business workflows, and Error-level logs for
every normal failed probe.

Avoid using health checks as a code-quality grading system and remote dependency
chains without operational justification.

canonical_policy.name: Normal client cancellation is not a server failure
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not map normal client-request cancellation to a generic 500 response or log it as an unhandled application failure.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Client-abort distinct from failure and timeout covered; no generic500/error log.

context_quotes:
Normal client-request cancellation is not a server failure: do not map it to a
generic `500` response or log it as an unhandled application failure.
Propagating `CancellationToken`: `performance.md`.

Treat client-aborted requests separately from unexpected failures. A
cancellation caused by `HttpContext.RequestAborted` is neither an unhandled
application error nor a `500`.

| Scenario | Default technique |
|---|---|
| Invalid HTTP input | Validation problem response |
| Simple query not found | `null` outcome; API maps to `404` |
| Multiple expected business outcomes | Typed outcome (Result only if adopted) |
| Unexpected exception | Global `IExceptionHandler` |
| API failure contract | `ProblemDetails` |
| Straightforward use-case/workflow rule | Application validator / Application Service |
| Non-trivial invariant genuinely owned by Domain | Domain enforcement |
| Recoverable external failure | Handle or translate at the owning boundary |
| Unrecoverable external failure | Propagate to centralized handling |
| Client/request cancellation | Propagate; handle as shown above, not as `500` |

This API acts as an intermediary and an upstream service did not respond in
time. Do not return `504` for every internal `TaskCanceledException`;
distinguish a client-cancelled request, our own operation timing out, and an
upstream dependency timing out — the correct response depends on which occurred
and on the role this API plays.

canonical_policy.name: API deprecation preserves the promised migration window
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: When deprecating an externally consumed API version, mark the deprecation in versioning metadata, document the replacement, communicate a realistic migration/removal timeline, and keep the old version working for the promised support period; do not remove it without considering the published support contract.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Metadata, supported/deprecated response headers, replacement, realistic timeline and promised support duties covered.

context_quotes:
Deprecation is a migration process, not merely an attribute. Mark a version
deprecated in metadata, for example `[ApiVersion("1.0", Deprecated = true)]`,
and with `ReportApiVersions = true` clients receive the supported and deprecated
versions in response headers.

When versions coexist, test meaningful differences: version routing,
version-specific response shape, a deprecated version still operational during
its support period, unsupported-version behavior, and shared Application
behavior staying consistent where intended. Do not duplicate identical tests
because two versions share Application behavior.

- When deprecating an externally consumed API version, mark it deprecated in
  the versioning metadata, document the replacement version, communicate a
  realistic migration and removal timeline to consumers, and keep the old
  version working for the promised support period. Do not remove it without
  considering its published support contract. Technique: `api-versioning`.
